summary: This RFC reproduces a draft of the ISO transport protocol that was being standardized at the time, previously printed in a 1982 journal. It was published for information, and the RFC itself says that version is out of date. It was replaced by RFC 905.

eli5.summary: This is a copy of an early draft of another group's rulebook for delivering data. The draft got old, so a newer copy replaced it.

subtitle: A draft specification for the ISO protocol that moves data reliably across networks.

tldr.problem: The ISO standardization effort was developing a transport protocol to provide reliable data transfer for OSI systems, but an early draft specification needed to be shared for information and feedback.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 892 reproduces the ISO Transport Protocol specification from an International Standards Organization working group, defining five classes of procedures for different network qualities and requirements, along with protocol mechanisms, data unit formats, and conformance criteria.
tldr.outcome: This draft specification was published as an RFC for information only, with the caveat that the version documented was already out of date. It was succeeded by RFC 905 with updated content.

today: RFC 892 documents an early draft of the ISO Transport Protocol and was published for information only, not as an internet standard. It was superseded by RFC 905. The protocol influenced OSI-based systems, while TCP/IP became the dominant protocol suite for the internet.

sections.title: The ISO Transport Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 892 publishes a draft specification of the ISO Transport Protocol, developed by the International Standards Organization's TC97/SC16 working group. The protocol is part of the ISO Reference Model for Open Systems Interconnection (OSI), which defines how computers in different environments can interconnect and exchange data.

The transport protocol sits in the transport layer of the OSI model, above the network layer and below the session layer. It bridges the gap between the services available from the underlying network and the services required by application programs using the transport layer. Unlike TCP, which was designed specifically for the internet, the ISO protocol was designed to work with any network underneath, whether reliable or error-prone.
sections.eli5: The ISO Transport Protocol is an international standard for reliably sending data across a network. It was written to work with many different kinds of networks, not just one kind.

sections.title: Service Model and Functions
sections.content:
The ISO Transport Protocol provides connection-oriented services, meaning applications establish a connection before transferring data, then disconnect when done. Service primitives (commands) allow a transport user to request connections, send and receive data, send expedited data (urgent messages), and disconnect.

The protocol assumes certain services from the network layer below it, such as the ability to establish and terminate network connections, send data, and optionally send expedited data. Depending on the assumed network services, the transport layer adds functions to enhance quality of service: segmentation and reassembly (breaking large messages into smaller pieces), multiplexing (sharing a network connection between multiple transport connections), flow control (preventing data from overwhelming the receiver), error detection and recovery, and expedited data transfer (bypassing normal flow control for urgent messages).
sections.eli5: The protocol works in three phases: first you set up a connection, then you send data back and forth, then you close the connection. The protocol can break big messages into pieces, pack several messages together, or handle urgent messages that skip the line.

sections.title: Five Classes of Protocol Procedures
sections.content:
A key innovation of the ISO Transport Protocol is that it defines five classes of procedures, each optimized for different network qualities and cost considerations. Class 0 is the simplest, assuming a reliable network with no errors. Class 1 adds basic error recovery, retransmitting lost messages. Class 2 adds multiplexing, allowing multiple transport connections on one network connection. Class 3 combines error recovery and multiplexing for networks with both problems and the need for efficiency. Class 4 provides full error detection and recovery, assuming an unreliable network that loses, duplicates, or reorders data.

Implementations negotiate which class to use during connection establishment, based on what the application needs and what quality of service the underlying network provides. This allows simple implementations for reliable networks and robust implementations for unreliable ones, all while remaining compatible with the standard.
sections.eli5: The protocol comes in five flavors. If your network never loses data, use Class 0, which is simple and fast. If it loses data sometimes, use Class 1, 3, or 4, which can fix problems. If you want to pack multiple conversations onto one network link, use Class 2 or 3. You pick which flavor you need.

sections.title: Protocol Mechanisms and Data Units
sections.content:
The protocol operates through exchanges of Transport Protocol Data Units (TPDUs), which are the packets of information sent between transport entities. Ten types of TPDUs are defined: Connection Request (CR), Connection Confirm (CC), Disconnect Request (DR), Disconnect Confirm (DC), Data (DT), Expedited Data (ED), Data Acknowledge (AK), Expedited Acknowledge (EA), Reject (RJ), and Error (ERR).

Key mechanisms include: connection establishment (sending CR and receiving CC), data transfer with optional acknowledgements and flow control using credit-based windows, expedited data with separate flow control, segmentation to map long TSDUs (transport service data units) to multiple TPDUs, concatenation to combine multiple TPDUs into one network packet, resynchronization to recover from errors, and graceful release to close connections cleanly.
sections.eli5: The protocol sends ten kinds of messages: some for setting up and closing connections, some for regular data, some for urgent data, and some for saying 'I got your message' or 'something went wrong'. Big messages get chopped up into pieces, and pieces get packed together to save space.

sections.title: Encoding and Conformance
sections.content:
The specification defines how all TPDUs and fields are encoded in bytes for transmission. Each TPDU begins with a length indicator and an octet describing the TPDU type and format. Different TPDU types contain different fields: for instance, a Connection Request carries addressing information and protocol class negotiation parameters, while a Data TPDU carries a sequence number, end-of-message flag, and the actual data.

The specification emphasizes that conforming implementations do not need to support all features. A minimally conforming implementation might support only one protocol class and omit optional functions, but any two compliant implementations should be able to communicate by negotiating compatible options. The document provides detailed state machines and rules for when each TPDU may be sent or received, recognizing that testing all possible protocol sequences is impractical but that the standard can be used to debug incompatibilities when two implementations fail to communicate.
sections.eli5: The protocol specifies exactly how every message is laid out in bytes so that any computer can read it. Different message types have different fields in different orders. Computers don't have to support every feature, but they must support enough to understand each other.

sections.title: Status and Context
sections.content:
RFC 892 was published in December 1983 for information only, carrying no standards status for the internet. The RFC itself notes that the version documented was from a 1982 publication and was already out of date at the time of publication. The ISO standards effort continued in parallel to the internet TCP/IP work, with different goals: TCP/IP was optimized for best-effort networks and became the internet standard, while the ISO protocol was designed to work with diverse network types under the OSI architecture.

RFC 892 was succeeded by RFC 905, which provided updated material. Today, while the TCP/IP stack dominates the internet, the ISO Transport Protocol remains part of OSI-based systems and influenced the design principles for reliable data transfer protocols.
sections.eli5: This RFC was published just to share what the standards group was working on, not to make it an internet standard. At the time it was published, it was already outdated because the standards group had moved on. A newer version came out in RFC 905. TCP ended up winning the internet, but the ISO protocol was used in other networks.

viz.caption: Five protocol classes for different network conditions

items.title: Class 0
items.text: Simple class for reliable networks with no errors.

items.title: Class 1
items.text: Basic error recovery for networks that lose some data.

items.title: Class 2
items.text: Multiplexing class to share one network connection efficiently.

items.title: Class 3
items.text: Error recovery and multiplexing for complex networks.

items.title: Class 4
items.text: Full error detection and recovery for unreliable networks.
